**Two up quarks and one down quark**
The standard giveaway: the proton is a baryon (a hadron made of three quarks) with two up quarks and one down quark, giving it a charge of +1. The neutron, by contrast, is one up and two down quarks. Protons and neutrons are held together in the nucleus by the strong force.

**Proton decay (to a positron and a neutral pion)**
Grand unified theories, and earlier Andrei Sakharov's work on why the universe has more matter than antimatter, predict that protons may eventually decay, most commonly into a positron and a neutral pion. This has never been observed. Experiments such as Super-Kamiokande, a huge water Cherenkov detector, have pushed the lower limit on the proton's lifetime above about 10³⁴ years.

**Proton-proton chain**
The main fusion process in the cores of the Sun and other low-mass stars. In its first step, two protons fuse into deuterium, releasing a positron and a neutrino. Overall, four protons become one helium-4 nucleus. In more massive stars, the CNO (Bethe-Weizsäcker) cycle dominates; its slowest step is the capture of a proton by nitrogen-14.

**Cosmic rays (about 90% protons)**
Roughly 90% of cosmic-ray particles are protons, with most of the rest being helium nuclei (alpha particles). Cosmic-ray protons hitting Earth's atmosphere produce showers of secondary particles, which led to the discovery of the muon and the pion. The GZK limit is the theoretical maximum energy of cosmic-ray protons reaching us from distant sources, because higher-energy protons lose energy by interacting with the cosmic microwave background. Large solar flares also accelerate protons toward Earth.

**Proton spin crisis**
In 1987 the European Muon Collaboration (EMC), scattering muons off protons, found that the spins of the proton's quarks account for only a small fraction of its total spin of 1/2. Explaining the rest, from gluon spin and orbital angular momentum, remains an open problem.

**Proton radius puzzle**
In 2010 Randolf Pohl's group measured the Lamb shift in muonic hydrogen (a proton orbited by a muon) and found a proton charge radius about 4% smaller than earlier values from ordinary hydrogen and electron scattering. Later measurements, including a 2019 result of about 0.833 femtometers, have generally supported the smaller value.

**Atomic number (Z)**
The number of protons in a nucleus is the atomic number Z, which defines the element. All isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. A nucleus with too many protons relative to neutrons is unstable because of their electrostatic repulsion.

**Beta decay and electron capture**
In beta-minus decay, a neutron turns into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino, so the proton is the heaviest product. In beta-plus decay, a proton (inside a nucleus) turns into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino, as one up quark becomes a down quark. In electron capture, a proton absorbs an inner-shell electron and becomes a neutron, emitting a neutrino.

**Antiproton (Segrè and Chamberlain)**
Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain discovered the antiproton in 1955 at the Bevatron in Berkeley and won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. Later, CERN's UA1 and UA2 experiments collided protons with antiprotons, which led to the discovery of the W and Z bosons.

**Rutherford's discovery**
Ernest Rutherford identified the proton around 1917-1919 when he bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles and found that hydrogen nuclei were emitted. It was the first artificial nuclear transmutation.

**Hydrogen ion (H+) and Brønsted-Lowry acids**
A proton is a hydrogen-1 atom stripped of its electron, the simplest cation. Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors, and Arrhenius acids release H+ in water. A proton attached to a water molecule forms the hydronium ion, H3O+. The standard hydrogen electrode, which reduces protons to hydrogen gas, is defined as having a reduction potential of zero.

**Grotthuss mechanism and Eigen cation**
Protons move unusually fast through water by the Grotthuss mechanism: a proton "hops" along a chain of hydrogen-bonded water molecules instead of one ion physically traveling the whole way. Key structures include the Eigen cation, H9O4+ (a hydronium surrounded by three water molecules), and the Zundel cation, H5O2+.

**Kinetic isotope effect and proton NMR**
Replacing a proton (hydrogen) with deuterium, which has twice the mass, slows reactions in which that bond breaks; this is the most common example of the kinetic isotope effect. Proton (¹H) NMR is the most common type of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

**Proton therapy and the Bragg peak**
Proton beams are used in cancer radiation therapy because protons deposit most of their energy at a sharp Bragg peak at a set depth and have essentially no exit dose beyond it, sparing tissue behind the tumor.

**Mass ratio to the electron and proton exchange membranes**
A proton is about 1836 times as massive as an electron. In technology, proton exchange membranes such as Nafion conduct protons but not electrons in hydrogen fuel cells. The Large Hadron Collider collides protons with each other at very high energies.
